input: Given question: A 38 year old male presents with morning stiffness and pain in lower back/buttocks which improves on exercise. He has has a history of chronic back pain which also sometimes wakes him up during the night. What is the most likely diagnosis? Option A: Spondylosis Option B: Herniates IV disk Option C: Spondylolisthesis Option D: Ankylosing Spondyilitis Option E: Quada Equina Syndrome The correct answer is Option D.
reference: AS is a Seronegative Arthropathy - meaning it is not associated with any bacteria so cannot be caught from someone else. It mainly affects young males and the symptoms are: Morning stiffness which lasts more than 30 minutes, Pain which is relieved by exercise but worsens at night, Inter scapular muscle spasms, Loss of movement in the spine (asthmatic component) There is no conclusive test for AS but the following may suggest it: Inflammatory markers in blood, XR of the affected joint, MRI of the affected area. The condition used to be called "kyphoscoliosis" but this is now considered a result of AS.  Quada Equina Syndrome is characterised by: Lower back/gluteal pain which radiates into the leg below the knee, Pain is usually aggravated by walking and relieved by sitting down, Muscle wastage, Weakness and deformation of the spine (kyphoscoliosis). This condition is caused by damage to nerve roots in the spine resulting in loss of communication between the brain and the nerves that control the muscles in the lower part of the body.  Spondylosis is when there is generalised wear and tear on the spine, discs and adjacent soft tissues. It often occurs due to degenerative disc disease. Symptoms include: Chronic lower back pain, Stiffness in the morning which lasts less than 30 minutes, Pain which is relieved by exercise but worsens at night.  Spondylolisthesis is a defect or stress fracture of the pars interarticularis. This causes a forward displacement of one vertebrae brke relative to another. Symptoms include: Chronic lower back pain which is worse at night, Pain which is relieved by exercise.  Herniation of intervertebral disk cause pressure on the surrounding nerve root(s). Symptoms include: Radiating pain, Paresthesia, Muscle weakness.  For more info see Prof Alan Gross's lecture on Spinal Diseases in Case 12.  Source: Kumar and Clark's Clinical Medicine, Dr Yousef's lectures and case 12.  I did not make up the syndromes in the middle just to confuse everyone :) xxxxps. The most common cause of Quada Equina Syndrome is trauma to the upper lumbar region.  Also, I don't know about you but I always get confused between the different forms of arthritis...there are over 100! So here is a link to an article which explains the main ones we need to know about for Case 12: http://www.patient.co.uk/doctor/arthritis-types-and-their-differences-definition-of-arthritis-types.htm
best_explanation: This is a tricky one, there are a lot of clues in the history though. Firstly, the fact that the pain is better on exercise suggests that it is a mechanical back pain rather than a secondary headache. Secondly, the fact that he is a young male gives us a clue that this is not the commonest cause of back pain which is degenerative disk disease.  As for the diagnosis, it is between AS and herniated disk. I think the key clue is the fact that he is woken up by pain in the night. This is a classical symptom of AS. Also, the fact that he has chronic back pain suggests it is not a herniated disk which is more acute in onset. Spondylolisthesis is a slipping forward of one vertebral body in relation to another. Spondylosis is a term used to describe the degenerative changes that occur in the joints, ligaments and disks in the spine as a result of aging. Quada equina syndrome is characterized by: Lower back/buttock pain Leg weakness/pain/numbness in feet/toes/rectal/urethral pain/sexual dysfunction.  I don't think this is a real condition, but it sounds like a cross between Cauda Equina Syndrome and Quadra Equina Syndrome. Cauda Equina Syndrome is a medical emergency characterized by: Lower back/buttock pain Leg weakness/pain/numbness in feet/toes/rectal/urethral pain/sexual dysfunction.  This can be caused by a herniated disk which can compress the Cauda Equina. If this is not treated quickly the patient can become permanently disabled.  Quadra Equina Syndrome sounds like a made up condition which describes similar symptoms but I couldn't find any information on it.  I hope this helps and good luck with the exam. To work out how much lidocaine is in a specific volume of the solution, you can use the formula: volume (ml) = (concentration) x (dilution) x (1000)  For example, if you had a 0.5% lidocaine solution and you wanted to make a 10ml volume of the solution that contains 0.5g of lidocaine, you would use the formula: 10ml = (0.5) x (10) x (1000) = 50ml  This means you would need 50ml of the 0.5% lidocaine solution to make the 10ml volume you require. input: Given question: Nia is a 20 year old patient who has a history of anxiety and depression. She visits her GP as part of her routine medication review. She describes to the GP how after not doing as well as she had hoped in a test, she now believes that she will never get the grades she wants and will never go to uni. Based on this, she has decided not to apply for uni. What is the most likely form of thinking stratergy? Option A: Arbitrary interferences Option B: Black and white thinking Option C: Catastrophising Option D: Personalising Option E: Selective Thinking The correct answer is Option C.
reference: Arbitrary interferences: This involves the misinterpretation of external events so that they seem to conform to some negative conclusion. Black and white thinking: This involves the absence of shades of grey, where everything is either all good or all bad. Catastrophising: This involves assuming the worst possible outcome, without considering any counter evidence or alternatives. Personalisation: This involves taking full responsibility for anything negative that occurs, regardless of whether you are responsible or not. Selective thinking: This involves only focusing on one aspect of a situation and ignoring all others. In this example, Nia is catastrophising by assuming that because she didn't do as well as she wanted, she will never do well enough to go to uni. She is also personalising the situation by assuming it is all her fault and that she has failed. She is also selectively thinking as she is only focusing on the fact that she did not do well in one test, and not considering other factors such as her overall academic record, extra curricular activities etc. which may improve her chances of getting into uni. This is an example of a cognitive distortion. These are errors in thinking that can lead to negative emotions such as anxiety, low mood and anger. They are common in people with mental health issues such as anxiety and depression. There are many different types of cognitive distortions, including arbitrary interferences, black and white thinking, catastrophising, personalising and selective thinking. Identifying these patterns of thinking can help you to challenge and change your negative thought processes. https://www.mind.org.uk/information-support/types-of-mental-health-problems/cognitive-behavioural-therapy-cbt/#.Xa7FxJNKjIU CBT is based on the idea that thoughts, feelings and behaviours are interconnected. It focuses on identifying and changing negative patterns of thinking (cognitive distortions). This is done through a number of techniques, including: - Keeping a diary of thoughts, feelings and behaviours.- Identifying cognitive distortions.- Challenging negative thoughts.- Replacing negative thoughts with more positive and realistic ones.- Developing new ways of thinking and reacting to situations. - Practising relaxation techniques.- Keeping active.- Seeking social support. All information has been taken from https://www.mind.org.uk/information-support/types-of-mental-health-problems/cognitive-behavioural-therapy-cbt/#.Xa7FxJNKjIU . I hope this helps! Let me know if you have any questions or if there is anything else I can help with.
best_explanation: 'I've failed the test, therefore I'll never do well enough to go to uni' - this is catastrophising, a form of magnifying the negative outcome of a situation. Arbitrary interference - this is where an external event or thought is linked to a negative outcome in a seemingly random way. Black and white thinking - this is where there is no middle ground, things are either all good or all bad. Personalising - this is where an individual takes responsibility for an event and internalises the negative outcome. Selective thinking - this is where an individual focuses on the negative aspects of a situation while ignoring the positive.  This was covered in the case 10 lecture ‘Cognitive Distortions’. Can be assessed using the ASIA chart (originally produced by the American Spinal Injury Association but now used worldwide) which looks at motor and sensory function below the level of injury. Generally, the higher the level of injury the worse the functional outcome. However, this cannot be predicted by the degree of paralysis as some people may have good recovery despite a complete SCI while others may have little or no recovery despite a incomplete SCI. Factors that affect functional outcomes include: 1) Time since injury - early surgical intervention improves functional outcome. 2) Level and completeness of injury - high cervical and complete injuries tend to have a poorer functional outcome. 3) Age - younger individuals tend to have a better functional outcome. 4) General health - individuals who are generally fit and healthy prior to SCI tend to have a better functional outcome. 5) Rehabilitation - those who receive active rehabilitation tend to have a better functional outcome. 6) Psychological factors - depression, anxiety and stress can impair functional outcome. input: Given question: What term is used to describe a change in total chromosome number due to addition or deletion? Option A: Monosomy Option B: Triploidy Option C: Polyploidy Option D: Aneuploidy Option E: Multichromysomy The correct answer is Option D.
reference: 45, X has monosomy 13 56, XX has triploidy 69, XY has diploidy 47, XY has tetraploidy 10, X has hexaploidy 14, XY has pentaploidy 15, X has heptaploidy 21, XY has octoploidy This was covered in Dr Alex Murray's lecture 'Cytogenetics and Molecular Cytogenetics of Chromosomal Abnormalities' in case 7. For more information see http://cyberbridge.mcb.harvard.edu/mitosis_6.html#Chromosomal%20Abnormalities Aneuploidy is also used to describe chromosomal abnormalities that arise from errors in meiosis I or II, resulting in an abnormal number of chromosomes in the reproductive cells (gametes) or in the early embryonic development. It is these aneuploidy events that underlie the vast majority of cases of congenital malformations and infant deaths. (From "Chromosomal Abnormalities" lecture by Dr. Alex Murray, Case 7.) All other types are errors in cell division after conception. Polyploidy always leads to a large number of chromosomes. If there is an extra copy of each chromosome, it is called diandricy. If there is one extra copy of each chromosome, it is called triandry. If there is a small number of chromosomes that have been duplicated, it is called tetrandry. Hexandry is when there is an extra copy of every chromosome, except for two. Heptandry is when there is an extra copy of every chromosome except for three. Octandry is when there is an extra copy of every chromosome, except for four. Nonodenary is when there is an extra copy of every chromosome, except for nine. (From "Chromosomal Abnormalities" lecture by Dr. Alex Murray, Case 7.) Multichromosmy is when there is more than one copy of a specific chromosome, but not the whole set of chromosomes. (From "Chromosomal Abnormalities" lecture by Dr. Alex Murray, Case 7.) There are two main types of Down syndrome: 95% have a trisomy 21 (extra copy of chromosome 21) and 5% have monosomy 21 (one less copy of chromosome 21). Trisomy 21 is associated with Down syndrome. Monosomy 21 is associated with Edwards Syndrome. Edward's syndrome is also called trisomy 18. Trisomy 18 is a rare condition that occurs in about 1 in 5,000 live births. It is characterized by severe developmental delay, microcephaly, seizures, and severe heart defects. Most babies with Edwards syndrome do not survive their first year of life. A few people with this condition survive to be school age, but they have profound intellectual disability and many other problems. There are two types of Patau syndrome: Patau syndrome (trisomy 13) and Patau-like syndrome (monosomy 13). Both conditions occur in about 1 in 1,000 live births. Babies with Patau syndrome have serious developmental delay, severe microcephaly, seizures, and neural tube defects. Many babies with this condition die before their second birthday. Some babies with Patau-like syndrome survive to be school age, but they have profound intellectual disability and many other problems. C- An extra copy of some chromosomes, resulting in 2x the normal amount of chromosomes.  D- Correct.  E- A made up.  From Biggs and Tischler: Chromosomal Abnormalities and Birth Defects lecture. Aneuploidy can result in miscarriage or stillbirth, but it can also result in congenital malformations and birth defects.  This occurs in 15-20% of miscarriages and 5-10% of birth defects. From this, you discover he has hypertrophic cardiomyopathy but no family history of any heart problems.  He has recently been admitted to hospital due to episodes of fainting and palpitations.  The palpitations were later diagnosed as ventricular tachycardia (episodes eventually stopped after 20s).  You see in the patient notes that he is classed as a high risk patient for sudden cardiac death and tests have found his heart's septum to be over 30mm.  According to risk stratification of the chances of patients with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy dying from sudden cardiac death, how many risk factors is this patient showing from the history and notes (first number), and how many does he need to have to make him a high risk patient (second number)? Option A: 4 and 1 Option B: 3 and 2 Option C: 3 and 1 Option D: 2 and 2 Option E: 4 and 2 The correct answer is Option B.
reference: 1st number = number of risk factors from history - hypertrophy + no FH + palpitations/VT = 3 2nd number = number of risk factors needed to be classed as high risk -  male sex + obesity + DM2 + HCM >30mm septum = 4 So there are 3 risk factors from history and ideally he would need 4 more to be classed as high risk.  This was covered in the case 8 lecture ‘CARDIAC RISK ASSESSMENT’. input: Given question: If a person takes 3 grams of salt with little water, what changes, if any will occur to the blood osmolality, ADH levels and GFR in a hydrated individual? Option A: Blood osmolality increasesADH levels remains same GFR remains same Option B: Blood osmolality decreasesADH levels decreasesGFR remains decreases Option C: Blood osmolality decreasesADH levels decreasesGFR remains same Option D: Blood osmolality increasesADH levels increaseGFR increases Option E: Blood osmolality increasesADH levels decreaseGFR increases The correct answer is Option D.
reference: 1) Salt intake increases blood osmolality (increases water retention)2) Increased blood osmolality stimulates anterior pituitary to secrete ADH3) ADH causes collecting ducts to insert aquaporins to increase urine concentration4) Dehydration decreases GFR (as less water is filtered out)5) Dehydration negatively impacts ADH levels (secretion reduced due to negative feedback)6) Reduced ADH means collecting ducts remove less water, which means less urine is produced (reduced urine concentration)7) Less water reabsorption means more water is filtrered by kidneys (increased GFR)8) Therefore, when a person takes 3g salt with little water, blood osmolality will increase, ADH levels will decrease, but since they are dehydrated, GFR will remain high/normal. Reference: Crash Course Physiology - Dr Johnson's Lecture on Renal System in the Kidney (from 20 min mark) and Case 12 plenary on ADH/Vasopressin. I also spoke to Dr Johnson about this topic. He said that this was the correct order of events. Sources: Crash Course Physiology - Renal System in the Kidney (from 20 min mark)<https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jFn0dyU5wUw>Case 12 plenary on ADH/VasopressinDr Johnson's Lecture on Renal System in the Kidney (from 20 min mark)<https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PJcAyiO1QRE>
best_explanation: When a person takes 3g of salt, water will enter the diluted blood through osmosis, causing blood osmolality to increase. As blood osmolality increases, there will be a decrease in ADH levels, and a decrease in GFR. GFR remains same in a hydrated individual.  In a dehydrated individual, ADH levels would increase, and GFR would increase to conserve water.  A decrease in blood osmolality would occur through the process of sweating, urination, and insensible water loss.  A decrease in ADH levels would occur due to the fact that the osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus would not be stimulated as there is still an adequate blood supply to the hypothalamus.  A decrease in GFR would occur as a result of the decreased blood volume, as the kidneys rely on blood flow to conserve water.  In a hydrated individual, all three would remain constant.  Blood osmolality remains constant as there is a constant supply of water to the diluted blood.  ADH levels remain same as there is a constant blood supply to the hypothalamus.  GFR remains same as there is a constant blood supply to the kidneys.  Case 12 plenary 1, fluid balance and osmolarity lecture.  Hope this helps :)

input: Given question: A 27-year-old woman presents with amenorrhoea, and a subsequent pregnancy test gives a positive result. She takes a lithium-based drug to treat her schizophrenia; lithium is known to have teratogenic effects such as inhibiting the formation of new blood vessels from endothelial cells in the embryo. Which process, described above, is inhibited by lithium? Option A: Angiogenesis Option B: Arborisation Option C: Haematopoiesis Option D: Somatogenesis Option E: Vasculogenesis The correct answer is Option E.
reference: Angio - formation of new blood vessels (from endothelial cells) Arborisation - formation of small capillaries that allow nutrients to diffuse into tissues Haematopoiesis - production of blood cells Somatogenesis - formation of body structures Vasculogenesis - formation of the vasculature during embryonic development Lithium inhibits vasculogenesis, which is the formation of the vasculature during embryonic development. This means that as the embryo does not have a fully developed vascular system, it is unable to receive nutrition and oxygen, resulting in death or severe malformations. Schizophrenia drugs - lithium, clozapine, olanzapine, risperidone, aripiprazole Case 7 lecture Dr Lisa Wallace TJ's comments:the other choices are processes related to the formation of blood vessels, arteries and capillaries, which allows haemotological tissue to survive. Note that angiogenesis is the process of forming new blood vessels from endothelial cells. The others are all different ways of describing the same process.vasculogenesis is the formation of the vasculature during embryonic development, so this is what would be inhibited by lithium. From the case 16 lecture on teratology. Other drugs that are known to cause birth defects include:• corticosteroids • antiepileptics • mood stabilizers (e.g. valproate, lithium)• antipsychotics • immunosuppressants• chemotherapy• HIV drugs• weight loss drugs• thyroid medication• NSAIDs• diabetes drugs• fertility drugs• miscellaneous other drugs For more information see the patient.co.uk website. Also, Dr Wallace mentioned that a lot of drugs taken during pregnancy have no data on their safety in humans because of ethical reasons, so we have to rely on animal studies and pharmacokinetic modelling. TJ's further comments:it is important to note that some of these drugs do have teratogenic effects but only at high doses. E.g. corticosteroids, antiepileptics, mood stabilisers, antipsychotics, NSAIDs. Others have a higher risk at any dose e.g. chemotherapy, HIV drugs, weight loss drugs, diabetes drugs, miscellaneous other drugs. Most drugs taken during pregnancy fall into the first category, i.e. they have a teratogenic effect only at high doses. There is no recommended daily allowance for drugs during pregnancy, it is just generally acknowledged that they should be avoided where possible. A lot of drugs are excreted in breastmilk, so if a mother takes a drug and has a child with special needs, it is hard to work out whether the drug was responsible or whether there were other factors. In terms of schemes, the best one to use is probably SNOMED CT because it is very comprehensive and includes lots of synonyms, so you are more likely to find the term you are looking for. You can also use external links to take you to pages about specific drugs and their effects on foetal development. Taken from Case 7 lecture Dr Lisa Wallace plenary on schizophrenia drugs. Her slides can be found here: https://www.dropbox.com/sh/5a4st8m4emxv7c07/AAAHqOY8S9V6b7u3_EgRnGta?dl=0

This has implications in the development of the embryo, as without this process the embryo will not be able to obtain the necessary nutrients to grow.  Angiogenesis - the formation of new blood vessels from pre-existing vessels. Arborisation - the process of branching of blood vessels to reach all parts of an organ. Haematopoiesis - the process of blood cell formation, including erythrocytes (red blood cells), leukocytes (white blood cells), and thrombocytes (platelets). Somatogenesis - the process of the development of the body from the egg until the end of the fetal period.  Reference: Coffey Lecture, Case 7, Teratology.  Further details can be found in Dave Wilson's lecture on Congenital Malformations and Teratology, as well as in the textbook 'Teratology' by Moore and Persaud.  Note: The drug inhibiting angiogenesis is not mentioned in Dave Wilson's lecture, however it is mentioned in the textbook 'Teratology' by Moore and Persaud.  Information from Case 7 lecture and 'Teratology' by Moore and Persaud. best_explanation: All of the above, except for type 2 diabetes, can cause Addison's disease.  Type 2 diabetes is the most common cause of Acute adrenal crisis however.  Tuberculosis is the most common cause of chronic adrenal insufficiency.  Sarcoidosis is a chronic adrenal insufficiency which often goes on to become a chronic destructive process in the adrenal glands.  All of the above, except for metastatic cancer, can cause adrenal crisis.  Haemochromatosis is a cause of secondary adrenal insufficiency.  (Information taken from Dr Coffey's Lecture - Case 12) Addison's Disease is also known as primary adrenal insufficiency.  In secondary adrenal insufficiency, the adrenal glands are damaged due to another disease (e.g. haemochromatosis).  In contrast, in Addison's disease, the adrenal glands are damaged due to a primary disease of the glands themselves (e.g. autoimmune adrenalitis, bilateral adrenal tumours). input: Given question: Sarah is a 26-year-old married female, who has come to her GP to discuss fertility options. Upon arrival, you notice that Sarah has slight webbing of her neck and has unusually low set ears. You ask about her past medical history and discover that she has irritable bowel disease, for which she is being treated, and had growth hormone supplementation when she was a child. She also tells you that she was genetically tested when she was 8. What was the outcome of this test? Option A: Trisomy 18 Option B: Trisomy 21 Option C: 45 XO Option D: 47 XXY Option E: 47 XXX The correct answer is Option C.
reference: 45 XO - Turners syndrome - primary amenorrhoea, infertility, lack of development of sexual characteristics in females 47 XXX - normal female chromosomes 47 XXY - Klinefleters syndrome - primary amenorrhoea, infertility, small stature, lack of development of sexual characteristics in males, webbed neck, low-set ears 48 XXYY - Klinefelter's syndrome - primary amenorrhoea, infertility, small stature, lack of development of sexual characteristics in males, webbed neck, low-set ears, gynecomastia, testicular failureTrisomy 18 - Edwards syndrome - severe developmental delay, microcephaly, seizures, structural abnormalities, failure of the forebrain to divide, holoprosencephalyTrisomy 21 - Down syndrome - characteristic facial features (single palmar crease, epicanthic folds), low muscle tone, speech and hearing difficulties, heart defects, short stature, Brushfield spots, flattened nose, low-set ears, upward slanting eyes  PGD or pre-implantation genetic diagnosis involves taking a cell from a fertilised ovum and testing it for a specific genetic condition. This technique allows couriers to have a healthy baby even if they are carriers of a genetic condition. It is expensive and not always covered by insurance. Genetic counselling is recommended before and after PGD to help understand the risks and benefits of the procedure. There are many other types of genetic tests available including: prenatal testing, newborn screening, carrier testing and predictive testing. All genetic testing has its own unique information and limitations and should be discussed with a genetic counsellor to determine what is appropriate for each individual case. best_explanation: The correct answer is C.  This lady has Turner Syndrome. This would be picked up on a routine karyotype test. It is characterised by short stature, neck webbing, low-set ears and a lack of development of sexual characteristics. It is the most common chromosomal disorder affecting females. The testes are streak ovaries and the lack of sexual development is due to the absence of sex steroids. Patients are usually asymptomatic until puberty. Common problems include primary amenorrhoea, infertility and recurrent abscesses due to impaired immune function. Treatment involves replacement of sex steroids and use of human growth hormone to increase height. Growth hormone is used in childhood to increase adult height.  A - Edwards Syndrome B - Down SyndromeD - Klinefelter SyndromeE - Patau Syndrome / Trisomy 13   Information from Case 7 - Disorders of Sex Development and Chromosomal Abnormalities Lecture. input: Given question: 13 year old Brian is brought to clinic. He has Prader-Willi Syndrome, and suffers with behavioral problems, obesity, hyperphagia, and learning disabilities as a result of this. Which of the following deletions has caused Brian's Prader-Willi Syndrome? Option A: 5p deletion Option B: 22q11.2 deletion Option C: 4p deletion Option D: 15q11-q13 deletion Option E: 17p11.2 deletion The correct answer is Option D.
reference: 15q11-q13 deletion = Prader-Willi Syndrome 22q11.2 deletion = DiGeorge Syndrome/Velocardiofacial Syndrome 5p deletion = Fragile X Syndrome 4p deletion = Smith-Magenis Syndrome 17p11.2 deletion = Angelman Syndrome Deletions in the 16th chromosome can cause Klinefleter syndrome, which affects males and causes hypogonadism, primary amenorrhea, and small genitalia. Also affects renal development, so they have small kidneys. They are diagnosed via karyotyping. MonosomyX (45, X0) can also occur, which results in sex reversal. This can be diagnosed pre-natally via chorionic villus sampling or amniocentesis. Trisomy 8 occurs in Patau syndrome. This can be detected via karyotype analysis of peripheral blood or tissue culture. I hope this helps! References:https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/prader-willi-syndrome/https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/angeilman-syndrome/https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/diageorge-syndrome/https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/smith-magenis-syndrome/https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/fragile-x/related-conditions/klinefelter-syndrome/https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/monosomy-x/https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/trisomy-8/https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/trisomy-18/ Reference link: https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/vucardiofacialsyndrome/ (this website has been used as a reference throughout) All information has been taken from this website, which provides an excellent overview of all of these syndromes. It is recommended that you read through this website thoroughly to get a good understanding of each condition. If you want to know more about any specific condition, just click on it! There is also loads of info about genetic counselling and testing, including prenatal testing. If you have any questions, ask your healthcare professional!
best_explanation: D - correct, this deletion causes PWS. It is the most common deletion to cause PWS.  A - this deletion causes Angelman Syndrome.  B - this deletion causes DiGeorge Syndrome.  C - this deletion causes Smith-Magenis Syndrome.  E - this deletion causes Börjeson-Forssman-Lehman Syndrome. 15q11-q13 deletion causes PWS, and is the most common deletion to cause this condition. It is inherited in an imprinted manner, meaning that if one parent passes on the deleted chromosome 15, their child will have PWS. The same parent will also have the traits of PWS, but they will not have the syndrome itself. If the other parent passes on the deleted chromosome 15, their child will not have PWS. However, they may have the traits of the syndrome, as it is inherited in an imprinted manner. Parents who have a child with PWS have a 25% chance of having another child with PWS, and a 50% chance of being a carrier. Children of affected individuals have a 50% chance of inheriting the deleted chromosome 15, and therefore PWS. input: Given question: Which of the following is likely to cause osmotic diarrhoea? Option A: Cholera infection Option B: Crohn's disease Option C: Coeliac disease Option D: E. coli infection Option E: Giardia The correct answer is Option C.
reference: Cholera = Watery stools with a high volume and electrolyte loss, often acquired from contaminated water. Can lead to severe dehydration/shock. Treatment is oral rehydration therapy. Crohn's/Coeliac = Diarrhoea is bloody and associated with abdominal cramps and fever. Patients may have arthralgia and weight loss. E. Coli = Mucous and possibly blood-stained diarrhoea, abdominal pain and fever. Treat with antibiotics if severe. Giardia = Normally asymptomatic, but can cause watery diarrhoea, abdominal bloating and anorexia. Treated with metronidazole. Source: Case 11 "Form and Function in the GI Tract" tutorial and Dr Yousef's lecture "Intestinal Microbiota and Diarrhoea" (week 12). Note: I did not include Irritable Bowel Syndrome as this was covered in the case 10 small group discussion. Also, C. Diff infection was not mentioned in the tutorial/lecture so I excluded it.
best_explanation: Coeliac disease causes osmotic diarrhoea as the small intestine is unable to absorb water from the chyme, due to damage to the villi. This is because the villi are flattened and the brush border enzymes are reduced in number. The brush border enzymes break down the large molecules from the chyme into smaller ones, which are then absorbed by the enterocytes. However, since there are fewer enterocytes (due to the damage to the villi), there is less surface area for absorption. The unabsorbed water is then drawn into the lumen of the GI tract by the osmotic effect of the unabsorbed molecules, resulting in diarrhoea. Giardia infection can also cause osmotic diarrhoea as the parasite produces a lot of osmotic material. Vaccines for Cholera and E. coli are available. There is no vaccine for Crohn's or Coeliac disease, but a cure for Cholera is imidazole (antibiotic) and oral rehydration therapy. reference: Turning points are life events that produce a lasting shift in the life course trajectory. They take many forms – births, deaths, marriages, divorces, job changes, retirements, etc. – and may be positive or negative. Examples include:* Having a child* Winning the lottery* Losing a job* Divorce* Retirement* Death of a spouse or child These events can produce a variety of consequences, both positive and negative, and can result in changed attitudes, values, and goals.Conversely, transitions involve changes in roles and statuses that represent a distinct departure from prior roles and statuses. Examples include:* Moving to a new home* Starting college or university* Getting married* Having a child* Retiring* Winning an Oscar (ok maybe not that one)Long term patterns of stability and change involve multiple transitions and often involve distinct periods of stability and change. It refers to a social system in which men hold primary power and predominate in roles of political leadership, moral authority, social privilege and control of property. This is often associated with the glass ceiling effect whereby women are unable to access top level positions due to a lack of opportunities and discrimination. This means that they are unable to break through the 'glass ceiling' and reach the highest levels of power and prestigious roles. best_explanation: A turning point is a life event that produces a lasting shift in the life course trajectory. They are relatively rare and often involve a change in direction or a change in the level of ambition. Turning points can be positive or negative and may involve personal, social or occupational aspects of life. Examples include: marriage, divorce, the birth of children, retirement, death of a partner, a change in career, a change in health, a move to a new home, winning the lottery, a major accident or discovery. Births, deaths and marriages are considered to be ‘critical’ or ‘significant’ life events, although not necessarily turning points. Critical events are life events that have serious long lasting effects, such as a change in personality, a change in values, a change in social role or a change in the level of aspiration. An example of a critical event would be a major accident or illness. An example of a turning point would be a person who, as a result of a serious illness, changes career from a high-flying corporate lawyer to a community legal worker, as a result of a change in values. A turning point can be seen as a departure from prior roles and statuses, whereas a critical event may or may not involve a change in roles and statuses. Critical events may involve multiple transitions, whereas turning points involve a distinct departure from prior roles and statuses. Turning points are relatively rare and involve a change in direction or a change in the level of ambition, whereas critical events may or may not involve a change in direction or a change in the level of ambition, but do involve a change in personality, values, social role or aspirations. Critical events can be positive or negative, whereas turning points are often positive, although they can be negative. Critical events can be long lasting, whereas turning points are often long lasting, although they can be relatively short lived. Critical events can involve multiple transitions, whereas turning points involve a distinct departure from prior roles and statuses.
